prompt.context: Your client is a manufacturer of test equipment for electronics companies. This is a high complexity, low volume business, where products range from $10,000 to $1 million. Products are built from sets of standard subassemblies, which the manufacturer holds in stock. When customers order a product, the Sales department determines customer requirements and configures the product using these subassemblies.
prompt.question: Currently, the client holds 183 days worth of inventory on average. Best-in-class companies hold 39 days. The client would like you to help reduce inventories to 85 days or less. How would you go about achieving this?

clarifying_info.q: How does the production process work after an order is received?
clarifying_info.a: After the order is received, the client assembles the product out of subassemblies and base units.

clarifying_info.q: What are subassemblies and how are they made?
clarifying_info.a: Subassemblies are essentially circuit boards designed by the client. Manufacturing is outsourced, with a cycle time of approximately 1-2 weeks.

clarifying_info.q: What components go into the subassemblies, and where do they come from?
clarifying_info.a: Components fall in two categories of approximately equal dollar value: (a) A large number of standard off-the-shelf components purchased from distributors as needed, with lead times of approximately 1-2 weeks; (b) A smaller number of custom components designed by the client and manufactured in low volumes by large semiconductor manufacturers, with lead times of approximately 9 months and little opportunity for improvement.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost breakdown of a typical subassembly?
clarifying_info.a: For a typical subassembly, 33% of the cost is standard components, 33% is custom components, and 33% is assembly at the outsourced location.

clarifying_info.q: What delivery time does the client promise customers?
clarifying_info.a: The client currently guarantees 4 weeks delivery time upon order receipt.

Inventory is comprised mainly of base units (little dollar value) and subassemblies (high dollar value). There are only a few base units in the final offering, but the total number of product configurations with different features and subassemblies is as high as 26,000.
Some subassemblies move very fast, while others move slowly and occasionally have to be scrapped because a new version of the product is offered.

framework: Understand the supply chain end-to-end: raw components → subassembly manufacturing → finished goods assembly → customer delivery
Identify inventory drivers at each stage: standard components, custom components, subassemblies, base units
Benchmark current 183 days vs. 85-day target; quantify gap by inventory layer
Explore levers to reduce subassembly inventory: demand pooling, SKU rationalization, postponement
Explore levers to reduce component inventory: shift procurement responsibility, exploit outsourced manufacturer's purchasing power
Assess feasibility constraints: 4-week delivery commitment, 9-month custom component lead times

questions.prompt: Walk through the supply chain from raw materials to customer delivery and identify where inventory accumulates.
questions.guidance: Strong answer maps each stage: (1) custom components (9-month lead time, must be held in advance), (2) standard components (1-2 week lead time, lower risk), (3) outsourced subassembly manufacturing (1-2 week cycle time), (4) finished subassemblies held in stock by client, (5) final product assembly from subassemblies upon order. Candidate should note that high-dollar inventory sits mainly in subassemblies, and that 26,000 possible configurations means enormous SKU proliferation driving excess safety stock.

questions.prompt: What are the key levers to reduce inventory from 183 days to 85 days or less?
questions.guidance: Three primary levers: (1) Reduce the number of distinct subassemblies through platform/modular design — create subassemblies that cover a broader function set but activate only what the customer pays for; pooling demand across configurations reduces variation and required safety stock. (2) Shift standard component procurement to the outsourced manufacturer — if they already buy these components for other customers, pooling across their entire demand base reduces the client's need to carry standard components. (3) Postponement strategy — given the 4-week delivery guarantee, it may be feasible to hold inventory as raw components (not assembled subassemblies) and assemble on demand; this would reduce inventory cost by roughly one-third since assembly labor (33% of subassembly cost) is deferred.

questions.prompt: If the client shifts to holding raw components instead of finished subassemblies, by how much could the cost of inventory be reduced?
questions.guidance: Subassembly cost breakdown is 33% standard components + 33% custom components + 33% outsourced assembly. Holding at the component stage defers the assembly cost (33%), so inventory value per unit drops by approximately one-third. This reduces the dollar value of inventory carried, which directly lowers days-of-inventory on a cost basis.

math.setup: Subassembly cost = 33% standard components + 33% custom components + 33% assembly. If inventory is held as components rather than assembled subassemblies, only the component cost (66%) is tied up instead of 100%.
steps: Component inventory value = 66% of finished subassembly value
Reduction in inventory cost = 100% - 66% = 34% reduction in inventory value carried
math.answer: Holding components instead of subassemblies reduces the cost of inventory by approximately one-third (33%).

brainstorming.prompt: What additional initiatives could the client explore to further reduce inventory and improve supply chain performance?

categories.name: Demand management
ideas: Improve demand forecasting accuracy to reduce safety stock
Work with key customers on longer-horizon order visibility or rolling forecasts
Introduce incentives for customers to accept longer lead times in exchange for discounts

categories.name: Subassembly rationalization
ideas: Audit the 26,000 configurations to identify low-runners that can be eliminated
Design modular subassemblies that serve multiple configurations (platform strategy)
Implement ABC/XYZ analysis to distinguish fast-movers from slow-movers and manage each differently

categories.name: Supplier collaboration
ideas: Negotiate consignment or vendor-managed inventory for standard components
Push standard component procurement to outsourced manufacturer to leverage their pooled volumes
Explore blanket orders with flexible call-off for custom components to reduce effective lead time risk

categories.name: Process and operations
ideas: Implement formal end-of-life (EOL) procedures to scrapp obsolete subassemblies earlier and reduce write-offs
Set inventory targets by SKU tier (fast vs. slow movers)
Use postponement: configure-to-order rather than assemble-to-stock for slow-moving configurations

categories.name: Technology
ideas: Deploy ERP/S&OP tools to improve inventory visibility across locations
Implement real-time consumption signals from assembly to trigger replenishment automatically

recommendation: Recommend a three-pronged inventory reduction program targeting the highest-value lever first: (1) rationalize the subassembly portfolio through modular platform design to pool demand and cut safety stock, (2) transfer standard component procurement to the outsourced manufacturer to eliminate the client's need to carry that inventory layer, and (3) adopt a postponement model — hold inventory as components and assemble on demand within the 4-week delivery window.

Together these levers can plausibly close the gap from 183 days toward the 85-day target; the custom component lead time of 9 months remains a hard constraint that limits how low finished-goods inventory can go for configurations that depend on those parts.
risks: Custom component lead times (9 months) are a binding constraint — any configuration requiring unique custom components must retain significant forward inventory
Modular platform redesign requires engineering investment and may delay new product introductions
Outsourcing component procurement to the subassembly manufacturer creates dependency and requires contractual protections
Postponement may strain the 4-week delivery guarantee during demand surges if component availability is insufficient
next_steps: Conduct an ABC/XYZ segmentation of all 26,000 SKUs to prioritize which subassemblies to rationalize first
Engage the outsourced manufacturer to assess appetite and capability to take on standard component procurement
Pilot the postponement model on a subset of slow-moving configurations before full rollout
Establish clear inventory targets by SKU tier and implement a monthly S&OP review to track progress against the 85-day goal
